newsitem.title: UK: Orange Order calls off disputed N.Ireland marches.
newsitem.headline: Orange Order calls off disputed N.Ireland marches.

text.p: Northern Ireland's Protestant Orange Order said on Thursday it had called off all flashpoint parades across the province on Saturday to avoid serious loss of life.
The decision was announced in a statement sent by facsimile to news organisations and was greeted by leading Northern Ireland politicians with huge relief.

Lodges (local organisations) of the order said in the statement that the decision had been made "for the greater good of the province, the maintenance of the Union (with Britain) and to avoid serious loss of life".
The statement said the Protestant organisation would not hold parades on Belfast's Lower Ormeau Road and in Armagh and Newry. It would reroute a contentious parade in Londonderry.
The holding of the parades had raised widespread fears of fresh Catholic violence after the Order marched down the Catholic Garvaghy Road area of Portadown last Sunday.
Sir John Alderdice of the Alliance Party said: "It has required courage. These are courageous decisions. A profound sigh of relief will go across every responsible voice in Northern Ireland."
Gerry Adams, who heads the Irish Republican Army's political wing Sinn Fein, said in a statement that he welcomed the decision
"I welcome these decisions and recognise its significance," he said. "I wish it had been made earlier."
He was referring to last Sunday's Orange Order parade in Portadown which sparked the worst violence the province has seen for years.

The Order's statement blamed the violence on Sinn Fein and the IRA, which want an end to British rule in Northern Ireland and to reunite the province with the overwhelmingly Roman Catholic Irish republic.
Northern Ireland police chief Ronnie Flanagan, who met Orange Order leaders earlier in the day, said he warmly welcomed the decision.
Catholic residents associations in Belfast and Londonderry had called for a mass Catholic turnout to block the parades, which mark the most cherished date in the Order's calendar.
It marks a 1690 victory by a Protestant king over an invading Catholic monarch which ensured a Protestant ascended to the British throne.
